Buttigieg acted as a surrogate for Biden's campaign in the general election.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-202)[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-203) He delivered a speech on the closing night of the [2020 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_National_Convention "2020 Democratic National Convention"),[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-204) and also announced Indiana's votes during the convention's roll call.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-205) On September 5, 2020, Buttigieg was announced to be a member of the advisory council of the Biden-Harris Transition Team that was planning the [presidential transition of Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_transition_of_Joe_Biden "Presidential transition of Joe Biden").[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-206)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-207) Ahead of [the vice presidential debate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_debates#Vice_presidential_debate_(University_of_Utah) "2020 United States presidential debates"), Buttigieg played the role as a stand-in for Republican vice president [Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence") to prepare vice-presidential nominee [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris"). Buttigieg was selected to perform this role because of his experience working with Pence during their simultaneous tenures as mayor of South Bend and [governor of Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Indiana "Governor of Indiana"), respectively.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-208)

## Secretary of Transportation (2021–2025)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Harris_swears_in_Buttigieg.jpg/250px-Harris_swears_in_Buttigieg.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harris_swears_in_Buttigieg.jpg)Vice President [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") swears in Buttigieg as Transportation secretary on February 3, 2021.

### Nomination and confirmation

Following the end of his presidential campaign, Buttigieg was considered a possible Cabinet appointee in Joe Biden's administration.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-209)[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-210) After Biden was declared the winner of the election on November 7, 2020, Buttigieg was again mentioned as a possible nominee for [Secretary of Veterans Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Veterans_Affairs "United States Secretary of Veterans Affairs"), [Ambassador to the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Ambassador_to_the_United_Nations "US Ambassador to the United Nations"), [Ambassador to China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Ambassador_to_China "US Ambassador to China") or [Secretary of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation "United States Secretary of Transportation").[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-211) On December 15, 2020, Biden announced that he would nominate Buttigieg as his Secretary of Transportation.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-212)[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-213)[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-214) The [Senate Commerce Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_Commerce_Committee "Senate Commerce Committee") advanced Buttigieg's nomination to the full Senate with a vote of 21–3.[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-215) Buttigieg was confirmed on February 2, 2021, with a vote of 86–13,[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-216) and was sworn in the next morning.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-217)

### Tenure

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Secretary_Buttigieg_visits_Union_Station_%281%29.jpg/250px-Secretary_Buttigieg_visits_Union_Station_%281%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Secretary_Buttigieg_visits_Union_Station_(1).jpg)Buttigieg visits [Washington Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Union_Station "Washington Union Station") on his first full day as [Secretary of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_Transportation "Secretary of Transportation").

As Secretary of Transportation, Buttigieg worked on re-organizing the department's internal policy structure, including carrying out a thorough review process of rules enacted under the [Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump").[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-218)[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-219) For example, Buttigieg reinstated an [Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama")-era pilot program which ensures local hiring for [public works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_works "Public works") projects on May 19, 2021, with the goal of helping minorities and disadvantaged individuals. This program had been revoked in 2017 during the Trump administration, when the Department of Transportation returned to rules established during the [Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") administration, which banned geographic-based hiring preferences.[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-220)

Buttigieg addressed the African American Mayors Association in late February 2021 to discuss systemic racism. He argued that misguided investments in the federal transport and infrastructure policy had contributed to racial inequity.[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-221) In early March 2021, *[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")* noted that Buttigieg had mentioned [racial equity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_equality "Racial equality") in almost every interview he gave to the press as it related to his work at the [department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Transportation "United States Department of Transportation").[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-222) In late June 2022, Buttigieg launched a $1 billion Reconnecting Communities pilot program to establish racial equity in roads.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-223) Using money from the [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure_Investment_and_Jobs_Act "Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act"), the program aims to reconnect cities and neighborhoods divided by roads through projects such as rapid bus lines, pedestrian walkways, and planning studies.[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-224)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Pete_Buttigieg_hugging_Barack_Obama_at_the_COP26.jpg/250px-Pete_Buttigieg_hugging_Barack_Obama_at_the_COP26.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pete_Buttigieg_hugging_Barack_Obama_at_the_COP26.jpg)Buttigieg and [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") at the [COP26 climate summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_United_Nations_Climate_Change_Conference "2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference") in Glasgow on November 9, 2021

After the 2021 birth of his twins, Buttigieg took a [parental leave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parental_leave "Parental leave"). This became a point of prominent criticism and ridicule from conservative and Republican figures. Some political analysts have noted [homophobic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homophobic "Homophobic") tones to the attacks on Buttigieg's decision to take a parental leave.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-225) After conservatives criticized him for taking a paternity leave, Buttigieg declared that he would not apologize for "taking care of my premature newborn infant twins. The work that we are doing is joyful, fulfilling, wonderful work."[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Kindelan-2021-226) According to his department, Buttigieg had been on paid leave since mid-August 2021, where for a month he was "mostly offline except for major agency decisions and matters that could not be delegated", and he "has been ramping up activities since then", making many media appearances in early October 2021.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-227) The White House had approved Buttigieg's leave.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Kindelan-2021-226)

After passage of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, *[Insider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_Insider "Business Insider")* called Buttigieg "the most powerful transportation secretary ever", as the department now has $210 billion of discretionary grants to award.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-228)

President Biden named him to the White House Competition Council, which coordinated policies to promote economic competition.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Scola-2024-229)

#### Aviation

After serious issues that had occurred in United States passenger aviation in 2022 such as [Southwest Airlines' holiday meltdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Southwest_Airlines_scheduling_crisis "2022 Southwest Airlines scheduling crisis"), Buttigieg faced criticism for not taking enough action to penalize negligent airlines.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-230) Buttigieg subsequently directed the Department of Transportation to address monopolization and consumer rights in the industry.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Scola-2024-229) President Biden and Secretary Buttigieg launched flightrights.gov, an airline customer service dashboard that informs airline customers of the compensation they are entitled to after flight cancellations or delays.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Buttigieg_and_Biden_Look_to_Shore_up_Airline_Consumer_Protections-231) He also created a chief competition officer position in the department. In March 2023, Buttigieg opposed the proposed merger of [Spirit Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_Airlines "Spirit Airlines") and [Frontier Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontier_Airlines "Frontier Airlines") as anticompetitive.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Scola-2024-229)

In December 2023, the Department of Transportation imposed a record fine of $140 million on [Southwest Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Airlines "Southwest Airlines") for mass violations of [consumer protection laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_protection "Consumer protection") in 2022 when the company cancelled flights and left more than 2 million passengers stranded.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-232) On October 30, 2024, Buttigieg announced that a rule had taken effect requiring airlines to automatically provide refunds to passengers whose flights are canceled and do not accept another flight, as well as if paid services are not provided.[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-233)

Buttigieg supports The Junk Fee Prevention Act. If enacted on the federal level it would lower fees relating to spending money on some forms of entertainment, hotel rooms, airport related services, and travel.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Buttigieg_and_Biden_Look_to_Shore_up_Airline_Consumer_Protections-231)

#### Infrastructure

Buttigieg informed Congress in late March 2021 that the Biden administration was planning to prioritize the construction of the [Gateway Rail Tunnel Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateway_Program_(Northeast_Corridor) "Gateway Program (Northeast Corridor)") due to its economic significance.[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-234) The progress of the project, which was stalled by [President Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"),[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-235) was said to be moving faster, according to Senate Majority Leader [Chuck Schumer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Schumer "Chuck Schumer"). Buttigieg announced the [environmental impact assessment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_impact_assessment "Environmental impact assessment") of the project—which was largely seen as a sign of major progress on the project.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-236) Also, Buttigieg has served as a promoter of the [American Jobs Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Jobs_Plan "American Jobs Plan")[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-237) and the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-238)

#### Other actions

Early into his tenure, Buttigieg noted that the United States's actions surrounding [road traffic safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_traffic_safety "Road traffic safety") are lacking and suggested improving the design of roads. Also, while acknowledging how the United States fell behind other [developed countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developed_country "Developed country") with respect to bicycle and pedestrian safety, Buttigieg encouraged greater focus on human behavior in infrastructure policy.[[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-239)[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-240) Likewise, in March 2021, Buttigieg indicated he was open to [tolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toll_(fee) "Toll (fee)") on [Interstate 80](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_80 "Interstate 80"), but not the tollage of bridges, suggesting "big picture solutions" instead, like [a mileage tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_pricing "Road pricing").[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-241)[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-242) However, the Biden administration did not include a gas tax or mileage tax in the [infrastructure plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure_policy_of_the_Joe_Biden_administration "Infrastructure policy of the Joe Biden administration") it released that month.[[236]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-243)

In June 2021, the White House created a task force to address supply chain disruptions, with Buttigieg as one of its leaders.[[237]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-244) By October 2021, global supply bottlenecks had resulted in record shortages of household goods for American consumers. Buttigieg cited high demand and the pandemic as some of the causes for the disruptions, while predicting that the disruptions would "continue into next year".[[238]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-245)[[239]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-246)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Secretary_Buttigieg_visits_East_Palestine%2C_Ohio_%281%29.jpg/250px-Secretary_Buttigieg_visits_East_Palestine%2C_Ohio_%281%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Secretary_Buttigieg_visits_East_Palestine,_Ohio_(1).jpg)Buttigieg in [East Palestine, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Palestine,_Ohio "East Palestine, Ohio") on February 23, 2023

[On February 3, 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Ohio_train_derailment "2023 Ohio train derailment"), a freight train carrying [vinyl chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinyl_chloride "Vinyl chloride"), [butyl acrylate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butyl_acrylate "Butyl acrylate"), [ethylhexyl acrylate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2-Ethylhexyl_acrylate "2-Ethylhexyl acrylate") and [ethylene glycol monobutyl ether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethylene_glycol_monobutyl_ether "Ethylene glycol monobutyl ether") derailed along the [Norfolk Southern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk_Southern_Railway "Norfolk Southern Railway") in [East Palestine, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Palestine,_Ohio "East Palestine, Ohio"). At the request of state officials, emergency crews conducted a [controlled burn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Controlled_burn "Controlled burn") of the spill, releasing [hydrogen chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_chloride "Hydrogen chloride") and [phosgene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosgene "Phosgene") into the air. As a result, residents within a 1-mi (1.6-km) radius were evacuated. Buttigieg [tweeted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") on February 13 the Department would "use all relevant authorities to ensure accountability and continue to support safety."[[240]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-247) On February 23, 2023, [NTSB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NTSB "NTSB") released a preliminary report stating that the wheel bearings overheated, with temperatures as high as 253 °F (141 °C) above the ambient temperature.[[241]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-248) In the weeks following the derailment, the Transportation Department, under Buttigieg, did not move to reinstate the 2015 rail safety rule aimed at expanding the use of better braking technology, which the Trump administration had revoked. Buttigieg's Transportation Department was contemplating stripping down brake safety rules even further.[[242]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-249) Buttigieg has faced some criticism from figures on different ends of the political spectrum for his response to the derailment, receiving criticism from Democrats such as [Nina Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nina_Turner "Nina Turner") and [Ilhan Omar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilhan_Omar "Ilhan Omar") and Republicans such as [JD Vance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JD_Vance "JD Vance") and [Anna Paulina Luna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Paulina_Luna "Anna Paulina Luna").[[243]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-250) Former president Donald Trump also criticized Buttigieg for not having yet visited the site while conducting a visit of his own.[[244]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-251) In March 2023, Buttigieg appeared on CNN, telling the cable news network that he had failed to anticipate the fallout from the derailment and erred in not visiting East Palestine sooner.[[245]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-252)[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-253)

## Post-secretary career (2025–present)

In January 2025, news reports emerged that Buttigieg considered a run for [U.S. Senate in Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_Senate_election_in_Michigan "2026 United States Senate election in Michigan"), with the announced retirement of U.S. senator [Gary Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Peters "Gary Peters").[[247]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-254) Previously, he had expressed interest in running for the state's [gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Michigan_gubernatorial_election "2026 Michigan gubernatorial election") to replace the incumbent governor [Gretchen Whitmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gretchen_Whitmer "Gretchen Whitmer"), who was term-limited.[[248]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-255) From February to April 2025, Buttigieg served as a fellow at the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago") [Institute of Politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Institute_of_Politics "University of Chicago Institute of Politics"), delivering a seminar on campus every week.[[249]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-256) In March 2025, Buttigieg opted not to run for the U.S. Senate in Michigan in 2026, with sources saying that he was instead mulling a run for president in [2028](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2028_United_States_presidential_election "2028 United States presidential election").[[250]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-257)

Kamala Harris, the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee, reported in her 2025 book *[107 Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/107_Days "107 Days")* that she wanted to choose Buttigieg as her running mate, but decided against it. She chose to not select him due to concerns about Buttigieg's sexuality (combined with Harris's own background as a woman and racial minority) affecting the ticket's electability.[[251]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-258)

## Political positions

Main article: [Political positions of Pete Buttigieg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_positions_of_Pete_Buttigieg "Political positions of Pete Buttigieg")

During his 2020 presidential run and after, Buttigieg has been variously described as a moderate or [centrist Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrist_Democrats_(United_States) "Centrist Democrats (United States)"),[[252]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-259)[[253]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-260)[[254]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-261)[[255]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-262) a [progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressivism_in_the_United_States "Progressivism in the United States"),[[256]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-263)[[257]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Berman-2019-264)[[258]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-265)[[259]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-266) or a technocratic [liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism_in_the_United_States "Liberalism in the United States").[[260]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-267)[[261]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-268)[[262]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-269) In 2019, Buttigieg labeled himself both as a progressive[[263]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-guardian_helmore-270) and a [democratic capitalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_capitalism "Democratic capitalism")[[264]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Stracqualursi-2019-271) but has simultaneously downplayed this, saying "these labels are becoming less and less useful" and that political ideology has "never been less relevant."[[263]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-guardian_helmore-270)

### Infrastructure

During his 2020 campaign for the [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") nomination, Buttigieg proposed spending $1 trillion on U.S. infrastructure projects over the next ten years, estimating that the plan would create at least six million jobs. The plan focused on [green energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_energy "Green energy"), protecting tap water from lead, fixing roads and bridges, improving public transportation, repairing schools, guaranteeing broadband internet access, and preparing communities for floods and other natural disasters.[[265]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-272)[[266]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-273)[[267]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-274)

### Social issues

Buttigieg supports [abortion rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_rights "Abortion rights")[[268]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-275)[[269]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-276) and the repeal of the [Hyde Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Amendment "Hyde Amendment"), which blocks federal funding for abortion services except in cases of rape, incest, or if the life of the mother is in danger.[[270]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-277) He favors amending civil rights legislation, including the [Federal Equality Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equality_Act_(United_States) "Equality Act (United States)"), so that LGBT Americans receive federal non-discrimination protections.[[271]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-278)

Buttigieg supports expanding opportunities for [national service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_service_in_the_United_States "National service in the United States"), including a voluntary year of national service for those turning 18 years old.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Wren-2018a-163)[[272]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-279)[[273]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-280)

In July 2019, Buttigieg shared his "Douglass Plan", named after [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionist "Abolitionist") [Frederick Douglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Douglass "Frederick Douglass"), to address systemic racism in America.[[274]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Burnett-2019-281) The initiative would allocate $10 billion to [African American entrepreneurship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American_entrepreneurship "African-American entrepreneurship") over five years; grant $25 billion to [historically black colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically_black_colleges "Historically black colleges"); legalize marijuana; expunge drug convictions; halve the federal prison population; and propose a federal New Voting Rights Act designed to increase voting access.[[275]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-282)[[274]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Burnett-2019-281)

Buttigieg supports abolishing the death penalty,[[276]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-283) moving toward reversing criminal sentences for minor drug-related offenses,[[277]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Higgins-2019-284) and eliminating incarceration for drug possession offenses.[[278]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-285)

In 2019, Buttigieg called for the United States to decriminalize mental illness and addiction via initiatives such as [re-entry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_reentry "Prisoner reentry") programs.[[279]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-PeteForAmerica.com-286) Also, he aspired to decrease incarceration rates because of mental illnesses or substance use by 75 percent during his first term as President of the United States.[[280]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-287)[[279]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-PeteForAmerica.com-286)

### Voting rights

Buttigieg favors the abolition of the [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College")[[281]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Deconstructed-2019-288) and has also called for [restoring voting rights to felons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felony_disenfranchisement_in_the_United_States "Felony disenfranchisement in the United States") who have completed their prison sentences.[[277]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Higgins-2019-284)[[282]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-289)

### Campaign finance reform

Buttigieg supports a [constitutional amendment on campaign finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_finance_reform_amendment "Campaign finance reform amendment") to reduce the undue influence of money in politics.[[283]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-290) During his 2020 presidential run, in response to accusation of campaign finance concerns, Buttigieg's campaign told *[Newsweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsweek "Newsweek")* that he did not accept contributions from individuals and organizations such as corporate [political action committees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee "Political action committee").[[284]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Lemon-2019-291) In addition, Buttigieg's campaign emphasized that Buttigieg had included critical campaign finance reforms as part of his campaign platform, including pushing to overturn *[Citizens United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizens_United_v._FEC "Citizens United v. FEC")* and *[Buckley v. Valeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckley_v._Valeo "Buckley v. Valeo")*.[[284]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Lemon-2019-291)

### Statehood advocacy

Buttigieg supports [statehood for the District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statehood_movement_in_the_District_of_Columbia "Statehood movement in the District of Columbia"), and said that he would support [Puerto Rico statehood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statehood_movement_in_Puerto_Rico "Statehood movement in Puerto Rico") if desired by the [Puerto Rican people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Ricans "Puerto Ricans").[[281]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Deconstructed-2019-288)

### Climate change

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Mayor_Pete_at_Roosevelt_High_School_%2848891405907%29.jpg/250px-Mayor_Pete_at_Roosevelt_High_School_%2848891405907%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mayor_Pete_at_Roosevelt_High_School_(48891405907).jpg)Buttigieg at a town hall meeting in [Des Moines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Des_Moines "Des Moines") on October 12, 2019,  
with supporters holding signs saying "Climate is a Crisis"

During his campaign for the [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") presidential nomination, Buttigieg stated that, if elected, he would restore the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")' commitment to the [Paris Climate Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Climate_Agreement "Paris Climate Agreement") and double its pledge to the [Green Climate Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Climate_Fund "Green Climate Fund"). He also supports the [Green New Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_New_Deal "Green New Deal") proposed by House Democrats,[[285]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-292)[[286]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-293) [solar panel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_panel "Solar panel") subsidies, and a [carbon tax and dividend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_fee_and_dividend "Carbon fee and dividend") policy to reduce [greenhouse gas emissions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenhouse_gas_emissions "Greenhouse gas emissions").[[287]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-294)[[288]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-295)

### Economic beliefs

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Pete_Buttigieg_%2848646620607%29.jpg/250px-Pete_Buttigieg_%2848646620607%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pete_Buttigieg_(48646620607).jpg)Buttigieg speaking at the 2019 Iowa Federation of Labor Convention

Buttigieg identifies as a [democratic capitalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_capitalism "Democratic capitalism") and has decried [crony capitalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crony_capitalism "Crony capitalism").[[264]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Stracqualursi-2019-271) He has entertained the possibility of antitrust actions against large technology companies on the basis of privacy and data security concerns.[[289]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Lizza-2019-296) During the [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") primary, he supported deficit and debt reduction, arguing that large debt makes it harder to invest in infrastructure, health and safety.[[290]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-297)

### Workers' rights

In July 2019, he released a plan to strengthen union bargaining power, to raise the [minimum wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_wage_in_the_United_States "Minimum wage in the United States") to $15, and to offer national paid family leave.[[291]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-298)

### Education

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Pete_Buttigieg_%2849405503067%29.jpg/250px-Pete_Buttigieg_%2849405503067%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pete_Buttigieg_(49405503067).jpg)Buttigieg speaking to the Iowa State Education Association in 2020

Buttigieg's education plan includes a $700-billion investment in universal full-day child care and pre-kindergarten for all children from infancy to age five.[[292]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Keeping_the_Promise_for_America-299) Buttigieg has also proposed tripling [Title I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_and_Secondary_Education_Act#Title_I "Elementary and Secondary Education Act") funding for schools serving students predominately from lower socioeconomic backgrounds.[[293]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-300) Other goals include doubling the number of new teachers of color in the next 10 years; addressing school segregation with a $500-million fund; paying teachers more; expanding mental health services in schools; and creating more after-school programs and summer learning opportunities.[[292]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Keeping_the_Promise_for_America-299)

His plan for debt-free college has called for expanding Pell Grants for low-income students, as well as other investments and reversing Trump's tax cuts for the wealthy.[[294]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-301) Under Buttigieg's college plan, the bottom 80 percent of students with respect to income would have received free education, while the top 20 percent would have paid for at least some portion of their tuition.[[295]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-302) Buttigieg has opposed free college tuition for all students because he has believed universally free tuition unfairly subsidizes higher-income families at the expense of lower-income individuals who do not attend college.[[257]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Berman-2019-264) This position distinguished Buttigieg from his competitors in the 2020 presidential election.[[257]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Berman-2019-264)

### Foreign policy

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Pete_Buttigieg_VoteVets.jpg/250px-Pete_Buttigieg_VoteVets.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pete_Buttigieg_VoteVets.jpg)Buttigieg speaking with [VoteVets.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VoteVets.org "VoteVets.org") in 2019

In 2020, Buttigieg called for modifying the structure of defense spending,[[296]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-303) while suggesting that he might favor an overall increase in defense spending.[[297]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-304)

Buttigieg has said that he believes the [2001 U.S. invasion of Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan "United States invasion of Afghanistan") following the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks") was justified[[289]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Lizza-2019-296) but supported the planned withdrawal of American troops from the region with a maintained intelligence presence.[[298]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-305)

In 2008, Buttigieg wrote an op-ed in *The New York Times* calling on the United States to support the *[de facto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_facto "De facto")* independent [Republic of Somaliland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Somaliland "Republic of Somaliland").[[299]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-306)

In June 2019, Buttigieg said: "We will remain open to working with a regime like the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for the benefit of the American people. But we can no longer sell out our deepest values for the sake of fossil fuel access and lucrative business deals."[[300]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-307) He supports ending U.S. support for Saudi Arabia in [Saudi Arabia's war in Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabian-led_intervention_in_Yemen "Saudi Arabian-led intervention in Yemen").[[301]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-308)

Buttigieg has condemned China for its [mass detention of ethnic Uyghurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_re-education_camps "Xinjiang re-education camps") in [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang").[[302]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-309) He criticized Trump's decision to [withdraw U.S. troops from Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American-led_intervention_in_the_Syrian_Civil_War "American-led intervention in the Syrian Civil War"), which critics say gave [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") the green light to launch its [military offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Turkish_offensive_into_north-eastern_Syria "2019 Turkish offensive into north-eastern Syria") against Syrian Kurds.[[303]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-310)

#### Israel

Buttigieg is a committed supporter of [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel").[[304]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-311)[[305]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-The_Jerusalem_Post-2019-312) He favors a [two-state solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-state_solution "Two-state solution") to the [Israeli–Palestinian conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli–Palestinian_conflict "Israeli–Palestinian conflict").[[305]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-The_Jerusalem_Post-2019-312) He opposes [proposals for Israel to annex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proposed_Israeli_annexation_of_the_West_Bank "Proposed Israeli annexation of the West Bank") the [Israeli-occupied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli-occupied_territories "Israeli-occupied territories") [West Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bank "West Bank"),[[305]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-The_Jerusalem_Post-2019-312) and disapproves of Israeli prime minister [Benjamin Netanyahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Netanyahu "Benjamin Netanyahu")'s comments in support of [applying Israeli law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_law_in_the_West_Bank_settlements "Israeli law in the West Bank settlements") in Jewish settlements in the West Bank.[[306]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-313)

In an August 2025 interview on [Pod Save America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pod_Save_America "Pod Save America"), Buttigieg did not give a clear answer on whether he supported limiting [arms sales to Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel–United_States_military_relations "Israel–United States military relations").[[307]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Bacon-2025-314) He said, "I think that we, as Israel's strongest ally and friend, you put your arm around your friend when there's something like this going on, and talk about what we're prepared to do together."[[308]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Gilson-2025-315)[[309]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-316) Following widespread criticism for his comments, Buttigieg said he would support limiting arms sales to Israel, as well as U.S. recognition of [Palestine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestine "Palestine").[[308]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Gilson-2025-315)[[307]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Bacon-2025-314) In 2026, Buttigieg did not respond when asked by *[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")* if he would reject support from [AIPAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIPAC "AIPAC"), a [pro-Israel lobby group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_lobby_in_the_United_States "Israel lobby in the United States").[[310]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-317)

### Healthcare

Buttigieg opposed Republican [efforts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Efforts_to_repeal_the_Affordable_Care_Act "Efforts to repeal the Affordable Care Act") to repeal the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Colombo-2017-127)

In 2018, Buttigieg said he favored [Medicare for All](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_for_All "Medicare for All").[[311]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-318) During his presidential campaign, Buttigieg has promoted *Medicare for All Who Want It*, which includes a [public option](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_option "Public option") for health insurance.[[312]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-319)[[313]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-320)[[314]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Transcript-321) He has spoken favorably of Maryland's [all-payer rate setting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-payer_rate_setting "All-payer rate setting").[[315]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-C-SPAN-2019-322) Buttigieg has described Medicare for All Who Want It as inclusive, more efficient than the current system, and a possible precursor or "glide path" to [single-payer health insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-payer_health_insurance "Single-payer health insurance").[[315]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-C-SPAN-2019-322)[[314]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Transcript-321) He also favors a partial expansion of Medicare that would allow Americans ages 50 to 64 to buy into [Medicare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(United_States) "Medicare (United States)"), and supports proposed legislation, the Family and Medical Insurance Leave Act, that would "create a fund to guarantee up to 12 weeks of partial income for workers to care for newborn children or family members with serious illnesses."[[316]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-323)

In August 2019, Buttigieg released a $300 billion plan to expand mental health care services and fight addiction.[[317]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-324)[[279]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-PeteForAmerica.com-286)

### Immigration

Buttigieg supports [Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deferred_Action_for_Childhood_Arrivals "Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals") (DACA) and repeatedly criticized the [first Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump")'s aggressive [deportation policies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_administration_family_separation_policy "Trump administration family separation policy"). In March 2017, he wrote an article for the *[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")* defending a resident of [Granger, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granger,_Indiana "Granger, Indiana"), who was deported after living in the U.S. for 17 years despite regularly checking in with [ICE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Immigration_and_Customs_Enforcement "U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement") and applying for a [green card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_card "Green card").[[318]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-325)

In January 2019, Buttigieg told [CBS News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_News "CBS News") that Trump had been "reckless" in sending American troops to the [Southern border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico–United_States_border "Mexico–United States border"), calling the decision "a measure of last resort".[[319]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-326)

## Awards and honors

Buttigieg was a 2015 recipient of the Fenn Award, given by the [John F. Kennedy Presidential Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_Presidential_Library "John F. Kennedy Presidential Library") in recognition of his work as mayor.[[346]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-353) To mark the [50th anniversary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonewall_50_–_WorldPride_NYC_2019 "Stonewall 50 – WorldPride NYC 2019") of the [Stonewall riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonewall_riots "Stonewall riots") in June 2019, *[Queerty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queerty "Queerty")* named him one of its "Pride50" people—"trailblazing individuals who actively ensure society remains moving towards [equality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_equality "LGBT equality"), acceptance and dignity for all [queer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queer "Queer") people".[[347]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-354) At the Golden Heart Awards, run by God's Love We Deliver, Buttigieg was awarded the "Golden Heart Award for Outstanding Leadership and Public Service" in October 2019.[[348]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-355) [Equality California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equality_California "Equality California"), an LGBT-rights organization, gave Buttigieg and his husband Chasten their Equality Trailblazer Award in August 2020.[[349]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-356) *[Attitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attitude_(magazine) "Attitude (magazine)")*, a British gay lifestyle magazine, named Buttigieg their 2020 Person of the Year to recognize his groundbreaking run for the presidency.[[350]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-357) In August 2024, Buttgieg was inducted by the [LGBTQ Victory Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ_Victory_Fund "LGBTQ Victory Fund") into the LGBTQ+ Political Hall of Fame.[[351]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-358)[[352]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-359)

The **United States secretary of education** is the head of the [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the president of the United States, and the federal government, on policies, programs, and activities related to all education in the United States. As a member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"), the secretary is sixteenth in the [line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession") to the [presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-2) Prior to its creation as an Executive Department, there was a non-Cabinet level position called the [United States commissioner of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Commissioner_of_Education "United States Commissioner of Education") who led the [United States Office of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Office_of_Education "United States Office of Education").

The current secretary of education is [Linda McMahon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon"), serving in this role under President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-3)

## Function

The United States secretary of education is a member of the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States")'s [Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States") and is the sixteenth in the [United States presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-4) This secretary deals with federal influence over [education policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_policy "Education policy"), and heads the United States Department of Education.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-5)

The secretary is advised by the [National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NACIQI "NACIQI"), an advisory committee, on "matters related to accreditation and to the eligibility and certification process for institutions of higher education."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-6)

Prior to the creation of the Department of Education in 1979, Education was a division of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare.

A partir da página do Wikipedia, posso identificar os secretários de Educação dos EUA desde o início de 2018 até o fim de 2024. Vou extrair a lista relevante, incluindo interinos.

De acordo com a tabela "List of secretaries", focando na seção **Education** e nas linhas que correspondem ao período de 2017/2018 até 2025:

- **Phil Rosenfelt** – Acting (Interino) – Virginia – de 20 de janeiro de 2017 a 7 de fevereiro de 2017 (antes da eleição de Trump).
- **Betsy DeVos** – Secretário (oficial) – Michigan – de 7 de fevereiro de 2017 a 8 de janeiro de 2021.
- **Mick Zais** – Acting – South Carolina – de 8 de janeiro de 2021 a 20 de janeiro de 2021.
- **Phil Rosenfelt** – Acting – Virginia – de 20 de janeiro de 2021 a 2 de março de 2021 (interino durante a transição para Biden).
- **Joe Biden** – Secretário (oficial) – Virginia? Na verdade, Joe Biden é o presidente; o secretário entre 2021 e 2025 foi **Miguel Cardona**.
- **Miguel Cardona** – Secretário (oficial) – Connecticut – de 2 de março de 2021 a 20 de janeiro de 2025.
- **Denise L. Carter** – Acting – (sem estado listado explicitamente, mas data: 20 de janeiro de 2025 a 3 de março de 2025) – Donald Trump.
- **Linda McMahon** – Secretária (atual) – Connecticut – desde 3 de março de 2025.

No entanto, preciso verificar a linha exata para 2018. O período de 2016–2017 incluiu John King Jr. (2016), Phil Rosenfelt (interino em 2017). Em 2017, Betsy DeVos assumiu após a eleição de Trump. Em 2020, durante a campanha de Biden, houve um interino? A página menciona:

- **John B. King Jr.** (2016)
- **Phil Rosenfelt** (Acting, Jan 20, 2017 – Feb 7, 2017)
- **Betsy DeVos** (Feb 7, 2017 – Jan 8, 2021)
- **Mick Zais** (Acting, Jan 8, 2021 – Jan 20, 2021)
- **Phil Rosenfelt** (Acting, Jan 20, 2021 – Mar 2, 2021)
- **Miguel Cardona** (Mar 2, 2021 – Jan 20, 2025)
- **Denise L. Carter** (Acting, Jan 20, 2025 – Mar 3, 2025)
- **Linda McMahon** (Mar 3, 2025 – presente)

Para cobrir 2018, o secretário em 2018 era **Arne Duncan**? Não, Arne Duncan foi em 2009–2015. Em 2017–2018, o secretário era **Betsy DeVos**? Na verdade, Betsy DeVos assumiu em 2017 e continuou até 2021. Em 2018, o secretário era **Betsy DeVos**. Mas preciso confirmar.

Vamos buscar especificamente a lista de secretários de 2018 a 2024.

# U.S. Department of Education

Election Day is almost here. Millions of voters rely on Ballotpedia. Help us inform them with a [gift today](https://donate.ballotpedia.org/campaign/856148/donate).

From Ballotpedia

Jump to: [navigation](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#mw-navigation), [search](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#p-search)

See also: *[United States education agencies](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_education_agencies "United States education agencies")*

The **U.S. Department of Education** is a United States executive department established in 1980. The department was formed to promote educational excellence and ensure equal opportunity for public schooling.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1) Of the 15 Cabinet agencies, the U.S. Department of Education has the smallest staff and the third largest discretionary budget.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-2)  

[Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") is the U.S. secretary of education. [Click here](https://ballotpedia.org/Confirmation_process_for_Donald_Trump%27s_Cabinet_nominees,_2025-2026 "Confirmation process for Donald Trump's Cabinet nominees, 2025-2026") to learn more about her confirmation process.

## History

Education in the U.S. is primarily the responsibility of states and local districts. The [United States Constitution](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution") does not mention any role for the federal government in education, and, according to the [Tenth Amendment](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution"), anything not mentioned in the [Constitution](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution") is left to the states to decide. A federal department of education was originally created in 1867 to help the states set up school systems by gathering information about teaching, schools, and teachers. The current U.S. Department of Education was established by [Congress](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") in 1980. It united several existing offices across different agencies into a Cabinet level agency located in the executive branch. Over the years, the location of the department in the government and its name has changed several times, and its scope, number of personnel and budget has significantly increased.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1)[[3]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-3)

The department's mission of fostering educational excellence and equal access arose out of the cultural and political events in the post-World War II era. The [National Defense Education Act (NDEA)](https://ballotpedia.org/National_Defense_Education_Act_(NDEA) "National Defense Education Act (NDEA)"), the first comprehensive federal education law, was passed by Congress in 1958 in response to the Soviet launch of Sputnik during the Cold War. The department added its "public access" mission in response to anti-poverty and civil rights legislation of the 1960s and 1970s.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1)[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-4)

Although the federal government provides only about 12 percent of the overall education spending of $1.15 trillion, the role of the federal government in setting education policy has grown considerably over the last several decades. The department implements laws passed by Congress and administers grants to states for certain programs, such as the [No Child Left Behind Act](https://ballotpedia.org/No_Child_Left_Behind_Act "No Child Left Behind Act"), [Race to the Top](https://ballotpedia.org/Race_to_the_Top "Race to the Top") and Title One School Improvement Grants.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1)[[5]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-6)

### Timeline

The following is a list of important dates in the history of the federal government's role in education:[[7]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-hist-7)[[8]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-8)

- 1862: The First Morrill Act provided the first federal aid for higher education by donating land for setting up colleges.[[9]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-9)
- 1890: The Second Morrill Act established a support system for land-grant colleges and universities.
- 1896: The [U.S. Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") case *[Plessy v. Ferguson](https://ballotpedia.org/Plessy_v._Ferguson "Plessy v. Ferguson")* legalized segregation in "separate but equal" schools.
- 1917: The Smith-Hughes Act extended federal aid to vocational education programs.
- 1944: The GI Bill authorized assistance to veterans for postsecondary schools.
- 1946: The Georgia-Barden Act established agricultural, industrial and home economics classes.
- 1954: The U.S. Supreme Court case *[Brown v. Board of Education](https://ballotpedia.org/Brown_v._Board_of_Education "Brown v. Board of Education")* outlawed segregation precedent set in *Plessy v. Ferguson*.
- 1958: The [National Defense Education Act (NDEA)](https://ballotpedia.org/National_Defense_Education_Act_(NDEA) "National Defense Education Act (NDEA)") supported loans for college students; improved science, technology and foreign language support in elementary and secondary schools; and provided fellowships in response to the Cold War.
- 1964: Title VI of the [Civil Rights Act](https://ballotpedia.org/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964 "Civil Rights Act of 1964") prohibited discrimination based on race, color or national origin in public schools.
- 1965: Title I of the [Elementary and Secondary Education Act](https://ballotpedia.org/Elementary_and_Secondary_Education_Act_of_1965 "Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965") gave federal aid to schools in poor rural and urban areas.
- 1965: The Higher Education Act authorized federal aid for poor postsecondary students.
- 1970: Standardized tests were given to public schools and the results were reported to the government and public in an effort to hold educators accountable.
- 1972: Title IX of the Education Amendments prohibited discrimination based on sex in public schools.
- 1973: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act prohibited discrimination based on disability in public schools.
- 1980: Congress passed the "Department of Education Organization Act," (Public Law 96-88 of October 1979).
- 2001: The [No Child Left Behind Act](https://ballotpedia.org/No_Child_Left_Behind_Act "No Child Left Behind Act") (NCLB) increased education funding and established standards-based testing reforms.
- 2010: The [Race to the Top](https://ballotpedia.org/Race_to_the_Top "Race to the Top") program encouraged states to compete for federal grants in education.
- 2025: Education Secretary [Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") announced the U.S. Department of Education would transfer the administration of some federal K-12 and higher education programs to the [U.S. Department of Labor](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Labor "U.S. Department of Labor"), the [U.S. Department of the Interior](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_the_Interior "U.S. Department of the Interior"), the [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "U.S. Department of Health and Human Services"), and the [U.S. Department of State](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_State "U.S. Department of State").[[10]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-10)

## Mission

The U.S. Department of Education's official department mission statement is as follows:

| “ | ED's mission is to promote student achievement and preparation for global competitiveness by fostering educational excellence and ensuring equal access. 
Congress established the U.S. Department of Education (ED) on May 4, 1980, in the Department of Education Organization Act (Public Law 96-88 of October 1979). Under this law, ED's mission is to: 
Strengthen the Federal commitment to assuring access to equal educational opportunity for every individual;
Supplement and complement the efforts of states, the local school systems and other instrumentalities of the states, the private sector, public and private nonprofit educational research institutions, community-based organizations, parents, and students to improve the quality of education;
Encourage the increased involvement of the public, parents, and students in Federal education programs;
Promote improvements in the quality and usefulness of education through Federally supported research, evaluation, and sharing of information;
Improve the coordination of Federal education programs;
Improve the management of Federal education activities; and
Increase the accountability of Federal education programs to the President, the Congress, and the public.[[11]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-11) | ” |

## [Noteworthy events](https://ballotpedia.org/Noteworthy_events "Noteworthy events")

#### U.S. Department of Education enters into agreement to transfer student loan portfolio to the Treasury Department (2026)

On March 19, 2026, Education Secretary [Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") announced the Department of Education would transfer its portfolio of student loans to the [U.S. Department of the Treasury](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_the_Treasury "U.S. Department of the Treasury"). These loans were worth about $1.7 trillion in total, as of March 2026.[[13]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-13)

#### U.S. Department of Education enters into two more agreements to transfer administration of some education programs to two federal agencies (2026)

On February 23, 2026, Education Secretary [Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") announced the [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "U.S. Department of Health and Human Services") and the [U.S. Department of State](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_State "U.S. Department of State") would administer additional federal K-12 and higher education programs through two further interagency agreements. McMahon said the State Department would assist in managing foreign gift and contract reporting for certain domestic public and private institutions of higher education (IHEs) as required by Section 117 of the Higher Education Act of 1965. McMahon said the Health and Human Services Department would assist in administering the following:[[14]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-14)

- the School Emergency Response to Violence (Project SERV)
- School Safety National Activities, Ready to Learn Programming
- Full-Service Community Schools
- Promise Neighborhoods
- Statewide Family Engagement Centers

#### U.S. Department of Education enters into agreements to transfer administration of some education programs to four federal agencies (2025)

On November 18, Education Secretary [Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") announced the [U.S. Department of Labor](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Labor "U.S. Department of Labor"), the [U.S. Department of the Interior](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_the_Interior "U.S. Department of the Interior"), the [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "U.S. Department of Health and Human Services"), and the [U.S. Department of State](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_State "U.S. Department of State") would administer some federal K-12 and higher education programs through six interagency agreements with the U.S. Department of Education.[[15]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-press-15)[[16]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-16)

McMahon said the partnerships supported President [Donald Trump's](https://ballotpedia.org/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") March 20, 2025, [executive order](https://ballotpedia.org/Executive_Order:_Improving_Education_Outcomes_by_Empowering_Parents,_States,_and_Communities_(Donald_Trump,_2025) "Executive Order: Improving Education Outcomes by Empowering Parents, States, and Communities (Donald Trump, 2025)") that called for closing the Education Department and returning its functions to the states.[[17]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-17) McMahon said, "The Trump Administration is taking bold action to break up the federal education bureaucracy and return education to the states. Cutting through layers of red tape in Washington is one essential piece of our final mission."[[15]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-press-15)

McMahon announced the following partnerships:[[15]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-press-15)

- **U.S. Department of Labor**: Elementary and Secondary Education Partnership
- **U.S. Department of Labor**: Postsecondary Education Partnership
- **U.S. Department of the Interior**: Indian Education Partnership
- **U.S. Department of Health and Human Services**: Foreign Medical Accreditation Partnership
- **U.S. Department of Health and Human Services**: Child Care Access Means Parents in School Partnership
- **U.S. Department of State**: International Education and Foreign Language Studies Partnership

#### Supreme Court allows President Trump's order to dismantle DOE to continue pending litigation (2025)

The [U.S. Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") allowed the Trump administration to resume enforcement of a March 20 executive order to shut down the Department of Education (DOE), pending the administration's appeal of a May 22, 2025, ruling by U.S. District Judge [Myong Joun](https://ballotpedia.org/Myong_Joun "Myong Joun") that blocked it. The May ruling also ordered the administration to reinstate fired workers. In a lawsuit, several education groups claimed that the Trump executive order hindered the department's ability to fulfill its mandated responsibilities, which include providing financial aid, supporting special education, and protecting civil rights. The executive order, titled "Improving Education Outcomes by Empowering Parents, States, and Communities," was written to shift education authority to the states and close the DOE beyond its "core necessities" of distributing Title I funding for low-income schools, money for special education, and Pell grants. On March 11, 2025, the Trump Administration laid off 1,300 workers, leaving the department with half its former workforce and most significantly impacting Federal Student Aid, the Office for Civil Rights, and the [Institute of Education Sciences](https://ballotpedia.org/Institute_of_Education_Sciences "Institute of Education Sciences"). Joun wrote that the layoffs "will likely cripple the Department," and noted that "the Department cannot be shut down without Congress’s approval." The Trump administration filed an appeal days later. The [U.S. Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") allowed the Trump administrative to resume enforcement of the executive order, pending the appeal.[[18]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-20)

#### Trump administration rescinds Obama-era guidance document (2018)

*See also: [Guidance (administrative state)](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance_(administrative_state) "Guidance (administrative state)") and [Rulemaking](https://ballotpedia.org/Rulemaking "Rulemaking")*

The Trump administration rescinded [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents in July 2018 that had been issued by the DOE under the Obama administration. The [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents encouraged institutions of higher education to consider race as a factor in the admissions process as a means to achieving student diversity. The documents provided legal recommendations and contextual examples for schools considering race as a component of the admissions process.[[21]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-cnn-21)[[22]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-wsj-22)

The decision to rescind the DOE's [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents occurred in light of an investigation launched by the [U.S. Department of Justice](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Justice "U.S. Department of Justice") (DOJ) in the summer of 2017 regarding allegations that Harvard University discriminated against Asian-American applicants by holding them to a higher standard than other applicants.[[22]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-wsj-22)[[23]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-23)

Attorney General [Jeff Sessions](https://ballotpedia.org/Jeff_Sessions "Jeff Sessions") announced the policy change on July 3, 2018. In his announcement, Sessions stated that the DOE is required to adopt new regulations through the [rulemaking](https://ballotpedia.org/Rulemaking "Rulemaking") process, which provides members of the public with the opportunity to offer feedback on [proposed rules](https://ballotpedia.org/Proposed_rule "Proposed rule") during [public comment periods](https://ballotpedia.org/Comment_period "Comment period"). He discouraged the agency from implementing regulations through [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents, which are issued by agencies in order to explain, interpret, or advise interested parties about rules, laws, and procedures:[[21]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-cnn-21)

| “ | The American people deserve to have their voices heard and a government that is accountable to them. When issuing regulations, federal agencies must abide by constitutional principles and follow the rules set forth by Congress and the President. In previous administrations, however, agencies often tried to impose new rules on the American people without any public notice or comment period, simply by sending a letter or posting a guidance document on a website. That's wrong, and it's not good government.[[21]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-cnn-21)[[11]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-11) | ” |
| --- | --- | --- |

Sessions previously instructed the DOJ to refrain from issuing regulations through [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents in a November 2017 agency memo. For more information about Sessions' DOJ memo on [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance"), [**click here**](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance_(administrative_state)#Presidential_administrations_on_guidance "Guidance (administrative state)").
